headline_marked: [[Pokémon Go Scans]] Train Navigation Tech for Military Drones
headline: Pokémon Go Scans Train Navigation Tech for Military Drones
summary: Hundreds of millions of player-submitted environmental scans from Pokémon Go are being used to train navigation systems for military robots, with a partnership announced for integration by December 2025.
details: Hundreds of millions of Pokémon Go players spent years filming the streets, parks, and buildings around them to earn in-game rewards. Those roughly 30 billion environmental scans are now owned by Niantic Spatial, and they helped train a camera-based navigation model that a U.S. defense contractor is preparing to put into drones and other military robots. Most of the players had no idea.

The pipeline runs from a mobile game to the battlefield in three steps. Players scanned the physical world. Niantic Spatial turned those scans into a 3D map that lets a machine locate itself by sight when satellite signals fail. In December 2025, Niantic Spatial announced a partnership with Vantor, the defense and intelligence firm formerly known as Maxar Intelligence, to fuse that ground-level system with Vantor’s aerial navigation software for use in GPS-denied operations.

Since 2021, Pokémon Go has asked players to record short videos of real-world locations, called Pokéstops, to earn extra in-game items. Scanning all the buildings, streets, and trees in a 360-degree sweep was optional, and Niantic asked separately for permission to keep the footage. Granting it meant agreeing to extra terms that handed Niantic a transferable, sublicensable license to the scans, meaning the company could resell the imagery to third parties.

Floris De Hingh, a 34-year-old Dutch player, told Trouw he never connected the footage he captured to a system that would steer military drones. "I was just playing a game," he said, noting he had even scanned the inside of his own apartment. The collected scans became the raw material for a Visual Positioning System (VPS), which works out a camera's location by matching what it sees against a detailed 3D model of the world.

Niantic Spatial CTO Brian McClendon, who previously led the team behind Google Maps, said the approach suits robots operating where GPS regularly drops out, such as dense cities, and where signals are deliberately blocked, such as war zones. The Vantor partnership, announced on December 16, 2025, joins Niantic Spatial’s ground-level localization with Vantor’s Raptor software for aerial navigation, enabling shared real-time coordinates without a satellite link.

Vantor, rebranded from Maxar Intelligence on October 1, 2025, is a prime contractor to the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency. The company is adding GPS-independent navigation to its catalog, targeting autonomous drones, vehicles, and augmented reality glasses for use in electronic-warfare-heavy environments. Field testing of the integrated system is planned for early 2026.

headline_marked: [[GPT-5.5 Beats Claude Fable 5]] on new Agents’ Last Exam benchmark
headline: GPT-5.5 Beats Claude Fable 5 on new Agents’ Last Exam benchmark
summary: OpenAI's model achieved a 24% pass rate on a new benchmark designed to test real-world professional workflows, surpassing Anthropic's latest offering.
details: Researchers have launched Agents' Last Exam (ALE), a new benchmark designed to evaluate AI's ability to perform complex, long-horizon professional tasks, moving beyond isolated coding puzzles.

In a surprising result, OpenAI's GPT-5.5 model, running on the Codex harness, topped the ALE Leaderboard with a 24.0% pass rate. This score surpasses Anthropic's new Claude Fable 5, which achieved 22.0% and placed third.

ALE focuses on real-world labor impact, unlike previous benchmarks that have been criticized for grading issues and 'cheating' by AI models. The benchmark uses a strict Generalist Computer-Use Agent (GCUA) framework, requiring agents to interleave shell scripting with point-and-click operations in desktop software.

The evaluation assesses AI capability across five layers: reasoning, visual perception, orchestration, tool invocation, and runtime substrate. Tasks are derived from the U.S. federal occupational taxonomy and include professional workflows like 3D model creation and SEC filing analysis.

While GPT-5.5's victory indicates a current advantage in adhering to complex instructions, the overall performance ceiling remains low. The hardest 'Last-Exam' tier saw most configurations, including older Claude and Google Gemini models, achieve a 0.0% pass rate.
The ALE project also addresses benchmark contamination by closely guarding its evaluation data, with only a portion released openly to mitigate the risk of models memorizing test instances.
